title: ‘Digger’: How Its Big Twist Saves the Movie From Being a Complete Disaster (Opinion)
description:
SPOILER ALERT: This story contains major spoilers for “Digger,” in theaters now via Warner Bros.

	When does a bad movie become a fascinating watch?
body:
SPOILER ALERT: This story contains major spoilers for “Digger,” in theaters now via Warner Bros.

	When does a bad movie become a fascinating watch?

	So often the kiss of death for a feature is boredom; that feeling you’ve seen the same story many times before, the actors are checked out, there’s no visual panache. That’s not the case with “Digger.” While it’s shaping up to be a box office disaster, the movie is anything but dull. Tom Cruise leads the cast in acting to the rafters, DP Emmanuel Lubezki keeps the camera moving and director Alejandro G. Iñárritu injects plenty of swagger in the proceedings.
	

	Unfortunately, the film’s opening — an extended introduction to Cruise’s ambitious oilman Digger Rockwell — is so in-your-face that it sags under the weight. Cruise is in grotesque prosthetics, eager to show us as quickly as possible how uncouth Digger is: He eats from the same can of sardines as his beloved cat, his butt crack is seen in plain view of his maid, his comb-over wisps wildly.


	It’s a clichéd character surrounded by other bobbling caricatures that enter and exit the rooms of his mansion, flailing wildly as Digger learns that his oil company might have inadvertently caused a climate-based global disaster. It’s shrill and tired, and despite the best intentions of the filmmakers to cause provocation around environmentalism, it’s about as subtle as Cruise turning to the camera and screaming, “DO YOU GET IT?!?” Ultimately, the poster’s promise of “a comedy of catastrophic proportions” seems more like a threat than a guarantee of “Dr. Strangelove”-esque genius.
	

	But then, an interesting twist happens. No, “Digger” isn’t a musical, but rather reveals that everything we’ve seen so far is a group of actors rehearsing an ambitious play about Digger called “Fossil Fools.” We’re witnessing the tech rehearsal hours before the show is set to debut in front of an audience, and Cruise drops his broad southern accent, revealing himself as Curtis Markson, the star of the show who has difficulty finding the satirical rhythm.

	It’s an engagingly meta turn, and shows much more of Cruise’s psyche than audiences might expect. During a teflon press tour hyping “Digger,” journalists weren’t able to conjure anything personal or interesting from him. But during a scene where Cruise argues with “Fossil Fools” director Hannah (Sophie Wilde) about satire versus real-world events, the artifice of Cruise’s fat suit and cowboy boots melts away, and the fire in his eyes that made iconic performances in films like “Magnolia” and “Eyes Wide Shut” blaze returns in flashes.

	It also helps to contextualize Iñárritu’s vision of satire itself. Some reviews of “Digger” have knocked the very idea of satirical films in 2026. After all, how can anything feel larger-than-life in the Trump era? But given the put-on-a-show staging, the film’s structure adds further firepower to standout scenes like Digger holding court in the United Nations, tap-dancing around a global community ready to feed him to the wolves after he doubles down on his wrongdoing.

	The showcase scene is emphasized by the fact that everything is underwritten by Digger’s real-life nephew Kenny (Jesse Plemons), who bought the rights to “Fossil Fools” and used his vast wealth to fund the production. His motivations are many, as he implies that he’s doing it out of a mix of penance, flagellation and tribute to his family name. But ultimately he’s a benefactor of the arts. The themes make it impossible to ignore the real-life soap opera currently happening at “Digger” studio Warner Bros., where new owner David Ellison swears he bought the company for all the right reasons.

	“Digger” ends on a somber note, with the audience methodically putting on gas masks and emptying the gorgeous theater, stepping into the dystopian world that remains after Digger’s environmental disaster. Flooded streets, discarded cars and military police are all around, until the camera tilts to the sky and the soundtrack becomes overwhelmed with the natural noises of wild animals. It’s a chilling wrap, as well as a dour end to what appears to be the last Warner Bros. film ever released.
	

	Not all of the elements tied to the twist work — Curtis’ search for his daughter’s missing flight during the tech rehearsal is curiously underbaked — but at least it teases a flurry of ideas instead of drowning in clumsy dialogue. At its best, it recalls Charlie Kaufman’s far superior 2008 film “Synecdoche, New York,” in which Philip Seymour Hoffman is a theater director who, in the pursuit of truth, creates a full-scale recreation of New York City in a warehouse in order to accurately reflect life. It, too, looks at the idea of understanding larger truths through a stage production, but is more clever and sincere.

	Ultimately, even the decision to add another layer, becoming a story about art just as much as one about the climate crisis, doesn’t escalate “Digger” into must-see territory. But the cross section of cinephiles who will be compelled to catch it in theaters — Cruise completists, flop aficionados, rubberneckers who want to see the world burn — will have more to chew on than the artifice presented at the beginning.

title: Skydance Says It’s Committed to L.A., but Threat to Leave Has Proved Potent
description:
Skydance is officially L.A.’s newest Fortune 500 company — but for how long?

	In a message to employees last week, CEO David Ellison said he is com
body:
Skydance is officially L.A.’s newest Fortune 500 company — but for how long?

	In a message to employees last week, CEO David Ellison said he is committed to keeping the company in Hollywood: “We aren’t going anywhere.”

	But the consent decree between Ellison and 12 state attorneys general does not require him to maintain a headquarters in Los Angeles. And the last two months have proven that the threat to leave can provide powerful leverage should Ellison need anything from state government in the future.
	

	“I think our attorney general and all of us were in a no-win situation when you had a company that seemed very willing and able to move out of California,” Rep. Laura Friedman told NBC LA. “I personally don’t believe that was an idle threat, and if that had happened, that would be devastating for Los Angeles.”


	Los Angeles has lost a series of corporate headquarters over the last 15 years, including Northrop Grumman, Occidental Petroleum, Toyota Motor North America, AECOM, SpaceX, Public Storage and KB Home. Companies often cite California’s high cost of living, taxes, and hostile regulatory environment in explaining their decisions to leave for Texas or some other state.

	“It’s a parade of horribles,” said Larry Kosmont, whose real estate advisory firm has long studied the cost of doing business in California. “If you had to fill a prescription for corporations leaving, California would get an A on the exam.”

	California leaders are also vulnerable to the charge that they have allowed companies to flee by failing to reform business regulations. 
	

	“Other states have improved in measures of tax and regulatory burden. California hasn’t improved,” said Sarah Bohn, vice president at the Public Policy Institute of California, who has found that corporate flight is indeed increasing. “The trend is not going in the direction you would want it to go.”

	In that context, losing Paramount would have been a powerful symbol, even if all that moved was a small corporate office. And that threat — even if Ellison has no need for it at the moment — remains available in the future.

	Under the agreement with the state AGs, Skydance will not sell either the Paramount or the Warner Bros. lots for at least five years. The deal also provides for increased production volume. The question of where the company will be headquartered was not included in the agreement, though it appears to have been discussed.

	“I believe that the future of this merged company is in Los Angeles for the foreseeable future,” said Attorney General Rob Bonta, in announcing the consent decree last week. 

	Ellison’s commitment, however, comes after he made a similar pledge and then went back on it in response to Bonta’s antitrust suit. In a letter to Friedman and Sen. Adam Schiff in February, Ellison vowed that the combined company would “stay true to our roots” in Southern California.

	The issue of what more must be done to keep film and TV jobs in L.A. remains a live one, both at the federal and state level. Congress is considering a U.S. incentive, while California lawmakers are expected to take up the question next year of whether to eliminate the $750 million cap on the state’s incentive, and whether to modify the program to include above-the-line costs. 

	“We’ve got to fight to keep Hollywood in Hollywood,” said Xavier Becerra, the Democratic nominee for governor, in a CNN debate this week. “And I’ve said I’ll do everything I can to make sure that happens.”

title: John Leguizamo Has a Message for David Ellison: ‘Think of What Americans Need and What the Industry Needs’
description: John Leguizamo is speaking out about the Paramount and Warner Bros. merger, and he’s imploring David Ellison to consider what the industry needs as
body:
John Leguizamo is speaking out about the Paramount and Warner Bros. merger, and he’s imploring David Ellison to consider what the industry needs as he takes over the new Skydance. 

	“Come on, Dave. Do the right thing. Don’t just think of yourself and your pocket. Think of what Americans need and what the industry needs. Think of others for a change.”

	Although the terms of the merger include Paramount-WBD being prohibited from selling the Paramount Studios or Warner Bros. lots in California for at least five years. Leguizamo said “that’s still not enough.”
	

	“You got an end date. You got an expiration date. That’s not cool,” he said. “People have to plan for the rest of their lives. They plan for five years, and then what?”


	“…The industry belongs in L.A.,” Leguizamo said Friday at the Critics Choice Association’s 6th Annual Celebración of Cinema & Television, where he was honored with the Career Achievement Award. “We need to support it and grow it. Rebuild it and add to it. Not subtract.”

	In April, Leguizamo was one of more than 4,000 film and TV stars and creatives who signed an open letter opposing Paramount Skydance’s pending acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery.

	“We are deeply concerned by indications of support for this merger that prioritize the interests of a small group of powerful stakeholders over the broader public good,” said the letter, which was published by the New York Times and available on the website BlocktheMerger.com. “The integrity, independence, and diversity of our industry would be grievously compromised. Competition is essential for a healthy economy and a healthy democracy. So is thoughtful regulation and enforcement.”
	

	Other signatories included Joaquin Phoenix, Ben Stiller, Kristen Stewart, Robert De Niro, Sofia Coppola, Florence Pugh, Pedro Pascal, Edward Norton, Atsuko Okatsuka, Adam McKay, Alan Cumming, Alyssa Milano, Boots Riley, Bryan Cranston, Cynthia Nixon, Damon Lindelof, David Fincher, Denis Villeneuve, Elliot Page, Glenn Close, Jane Fonda, JJ Abrams, Jason Bateman, John Leguizamo, Lin-Manuel Miranda, Margaret Cho, Mark Ruffalo, Noah Wyle, Patti Lupone, Ramy Youssef, Rosario Dawson, Rosie O’Donnell, Ted Danson, Tiffany Haddish, Tig Notaro, Yorgos Lanthimos and Yvette Nicole Brown.

title: Skydance Shuffle: David Ellison Addresses Troops About New Name, Says Adieu to Mike and Pam and Sets Table for ‘Barbie 2’
description: It’s 102 degrees in Los Angeles, but it’s certainly not a summer Friday on the Paramount lot. The studio is swarming with activity, subplots and pre
body:
It’s 102 degrees in Los Angeles, but it’s certainly not a summer Friday on the Paramount lot. The studio is swarming with activity, subplots and preparations for the closing of Skydance‘s acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery next week.The industry is obsessively speculating on who survives the merger to be named to David Ellison‘s executive leadership team come Monday. But first thing’s first — Ellison addressed his troops on the combined company’s new name. It’s Skydance, same as the company Ellison founded 20 years ago, and will be the parent to existing brands like Warner Bros., Paramount and HBO.“As we bring Paramount and Warner Bros. together, we wanted to preserve what has made each of these studios iconic. Both have distinct identities, extraordinary legacies and brands that have resonated with audiences for generations,” Ellison wrote to staff in a memo obtained by Variety. “We never wanted a new corporate identity to diminish, alter or overshadow either one. Instead, we wanted a name that would give the combined company an identity of its own while allowing Paramount and Warner Bros. — and all our extraordinary brands — to remain in the spotlight.”Remain they will, though under various layers of oversight. Paramount Pictures leaders Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein will be elevated to an expansive creative post, multiple sources tell Variety, overseeing heads of individual film labels across both companies (like New Line stalwart Richard Brener). With this week’s exit of Paramount+ streaming head Cindy Holland, Casey Bloys is the presumptive ruler of all streaming at Skydance. The company has yet to make anything official.Variety confirmed late Thursday night that Warner Bros. Motion Picture Group heads Pamela Abdy and Michael De Luca are out. The decision shocked them, insiders said, though another power player with knowledge of the duo remarked that if they were surprised, “they’re the only ones.” Their fate has been one of the biggest question marks looming over the entire deal. Timing wasn’t on their side, as the motion picture group stacked dizzying losses for WBD this year (despite a banner 2025). Another source added that Ellison personally spoke to the pair on Friday. Today is thought to be their last day on the Warner Bros. lot in Burbank.While Ellison won’t get the keys to WBD until next week’s formal close, dealmaking activity is surging. Goldberg and Greenstein have been reaching out to key talent at Warner Bros. (like Margot Robbie and her LuckyChap partners) to establish continuity. Another knowledgeable source said that wheels are already turning to lock in a sequel to Greta Gerwig‘s “Barbie,” which we previously reported had flatlined over costs. Keep in mind, Ellison just tapped former Mattel CEO Ynon Kriez to be the co-CEO at the new combined company.

	“There’s no way ‘Barbie 2’ doesn’t happen,” said the source.
	
	Team,I am excited to share the new name of our combined company, Skydance.We chose this name for a few important reasons. First and foremost, as we bring Paramount and Warner Bros. together, we wanted to preserve what has made each of these studios iconic. Both have distinct identities, extraordinary legacies and brands that have resonated with audiences for generations. We never wanted a new corporate identity to diminish, alter or overshadow either one. Instead, we wanted a name that would give the combined company an identity of its own while allowing Paramount and Warner Bros. — and all our extraordinary brands — to remain in the spotlight.Of course, Skydance also carries deep meaning for me. I chose the name for my own studio 20 years ago because I wanted something truly personal that also represented limitless possibility. The personal part came from my love of flight: skydancing is another name for aerobatic flying. The possibility came from the cosmos, which to me represents boundless potential and the large-canvas storytelling of cinema. Even our original logo reflected that idea, with each letter of Skydance representing a planet revolving around the sun. From the beginning, the name was meant to capture what great storytelling can do: transport people to places they might never otherwise go and take us beyond the limits of the world we know — and even our own imaginations. That sense of scale, discovery and ambition feels especially fitting for what we are building today.We have big goals for Skydance, and we intend to pursue them with passion, imagination and a willingness to take smart risks. At the same time, we will honor what makes Paramount and Warner Bros. special — giving both studios the opportunity to grow, tell more great stories and bring those stories to even broader audiences around the world, powered by the scale and capabilities of Skydance.Welcome to Skydance. I couldn’t be more excited about what we’re going to build together.David

title: European Entertainment Leaders Mostly Optimistic About David Ellison’s Takeover of Warner Bros. : ‘I Believe in His Commitment to Cinema’
description: After nearly a year of dealmaking drama, Paramount Skydance‘s takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery is about to become reality. Across Europe, where th
body:
After nearly a year of dealmaking drama, Paramount Skydance‘s takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery is about to become reality. Across Europe, where the Paramount chief David Ellison has spent time courting support for his vision of building a Hollywood colossus, the mood is surprisingly upbeat.

	The debt-laden $111 billion merger is set to close Oct. 6 after a federal judge signed off on Paramount’s settlement of the antitrust lawsuit filed by 12 states in July. 
	

	Under that deal, the company has strict obligations for movies and for theatrical exhibition. The combined company is legally obligated to release at least 30 films theatrically in each of its first two years and 32 a year in years three through five, with a 45-day theatrical window for wide releases and a 90-day hold before they reach subscription streaming. Paramount has also committed an additional $300 million a year, or $1.5 billion over five years, to U.S. film production.


	That last pledge matters for Europe, which has become one of Hollywood’s busiest production hubs and where the merger got antitrust approvals faster than in the U.S. The question that showbiz insiders are asking in the U.S. is the same for Europe’s industry heavyweights: Can Ellison keep the promises he has made to filmmakers, producers and exhibitors on both sides of the Atlantic if those commitments collide with the $79 billion in debt that the company will shoulder following the blockbuster deal.

	Pierre-Antoine Capton, co-founder and chairman of Mediawan, one of Europe’s top production powerhouses and biggest consolidators, believes Ellison’s commitments will hold.
	

	“In Europe, we’ve also entered a period of intense consolidation. Obviously, a transaction of this size is going to involve synergies, but having spoken with David, I believe his vision is first and foremost an artistic, creative ambition,” Capton tells Variety. “He wants to build a more powerful group in order to invest in creation, and it’s not only about making cuts. So I believe in his commitment to cinema and to theatrical releases.”

	As the head of a vast production group including North Road, Plan B and See-Saw Films, Capton is also optimistic about what belt-tightening will mean for commissions. 

	“You can obviously rationalize structures while keeping, and even increasing, your creative ambition. That’s what we’re trying to do at Mediawan, on a much smaller scale. I think everywhere in the world we’re entering a much more difficult phase, where consolidation will be, in my view, one of the solutions to the economic problems we’re all going to face,” Capton says. He added that he sees opportunity for a strong independents like Mediawan to offset the U.S. media behemoths, especially in territories where they don’t have boots on the ground.

	Ellison had been able to garner support from across Europe since he went on a lobbying mission on behalf of the merger at the start of the year, meeting political leaders and entertainment figures in France, Germany and the U.K. to rally support for his unsolicited takeover bid. Weeks later, he sent an open letter to the creative community pledging that the combined Paramount and Warner Bros. will release 30 movies a year in theaters.

	But not everyone in Europe, however, is convinced the business will survive intact. Prominent Italian production executive Marco Chimenz, former president of the European Producers Club, is skeptical.

	“Though Ellison has promised that the number of films the studios will produce will stay the same, if not grow, I doubt that’s going to happen, the same way it didn’t happen when Disney merged with Fox,” Chimenz says. “I think that a contraction in the combined number of films from Paramount and Warner Bros. is in order, and this will certainly be true when it comes to mid-budget films that will increasingly be destined straight to streaming or straight to television.”
	

	On television, though, Chimenz is more hopeful and believes the “impact of the merger might end up being positive in Italy and other European countries with respect to the business of commissioning TV series.” Paramount has not been very active in the international co-productions arena but HBO has. “HBO is playing an interesting role in the production of originals right now,” he says.

	As many producers and talents are hoping to see HBO even more engaged, Chimenz wonders whether “the merger, once it’s finished, will prompt the combined entity to invest more in local productions.” 

	The first reason, he says, “is that local audiences really love local productions, but also to fully comply with the rules determining investment in local content. So I hope that the result in this specific area will be positive.”

	The bigger worry for Europe may be physical production. Media analyst François Godard believes the merger, combined with the new U.S. federal tax credit, will mean that “Hollywood productions will move away from Europe, Canada and Australia and go back to shooting in the U.S., and specifically California.”

	That would hit hardest in Britain, where Warner Bros. shoots everything from the upcoming “Harry Potter” TV series to its DC movie tentpoles at Leavesden Studios. But U.K. exhibitors and producers are still confident the country has a strong enough track record and incentives and enough other perks to keep luring big Hollywood shoots.

	“We have such a thriving industry here, with so many experts, so many skills,” says Clare Binns, BAFTA-winning creative director of Picturehouse Cinemas. “People want to shoot here and I don’t think that’s going to go away. We’ve set ourselves up. Obviously, there’s always risk, but I think we’re in a good position.”

	Tim Richards, CEO of exhibition giant Vue and former chair of the BFI, agrees. “From the U.K. perspective, we have one of the best, most highly trained skill sets for filmmakers in the world. And we’ve got a great place to live. We’re a great place to shoot films. We’ve got the infrastructure built up and we’ve got a very attractive tax credit. So we’re not going to lose everything,” Richards says.

	Some knock-on effects in sports are also expected. Paramount+ is set to launch the Champions League in the U.K. and Germany in September of next year, but WBD already co-owns TNT Sports with BT. “Now they have the same ownership as TNT,” Godard says. “So they must settle something with BT to take over TNT and merge TNT with Paramount+. They will also have to reconfigure their sports offering in Germany.”
	

	When it comes to cinemas, however, Godard is upbeat. 

	“My feeling is that everybody’s interests are aligned in trying to relaunch theatrical exhibition. If you start squeezing out some films, you just undermine the ecosystem,” Godard says. “When you have big market share, at some point you find yourself tempted to leverage it, because if you have two big films to release and you want the best exposure, conflicts may arise. But the exhibition industry is very well organized, and I think they will draw a red flag if something happens.”

	Vue’s Richards, who was highly critical of Netflix’s efforts to buy Warner Bros. earlier this year, points to Ellison’s record at Paramount. “From a credibility standpoint, you look at what David Ellison has already done at Paramount, which had a run rate of seven to eight films a year and this year are going to be releasing 15 movies,” he says. “And that was before Warner Bros. was even on the horizon. You’re dealing with proper filmmakers and businessmen and not just businessmen. And that’s the difference.”

	Picturehouse’s Binns is also prepared to take Ellison at his word, but she argues the number of films is only half the story.

	“I would hope if he said that, then I would expect him to deliver that. But it’s not just the 30 movies. It’s what those 30 movies are. It’s what those hires are. It’s what he is now going to [do about] the breadth and range of films that I think everybody wants to see,” says Binns. “I think all the production in the U.K., big and small, will want to feel that there’s someone at the helm that is interested in the long-term survival of this industry, which means taking risks.”

	Binns raises the concern that Paramount may take a conservative approach to greenlights. She’ll be watching for the genres and the filmmakers that the new-model Paramount and Warner Bros. embrace.

	“The concern is who he’s going to be hiring,” says Binns. “He’s made one major hire, Ynon Kreiz, from Mattel. We just need to make sure that the hires are going to be reflective of what’s going on at the moment. If we’re just going to have white men doing their thing, that is just something that rings a bit of an alarm bell to me. And what we need is range.

	“We need the Danny Boyle films, we need the ‘One Battle After Another,’ as well as we need the big franchise movies,” Binns says. “If he makes 30 movies a year, that will be great. But it will be even better if he makes films that cover a broad range of tastes and what is actually reflective of a very exciting industry with lots of new voices.”

title: ‘Verity’ Had a Much More Twisted Ending. Then Came the Focus Group Screenings
description:
SPOILER ALERT: This article contains spoilers for “Verity,” now playing in theaters.

	To say that “Verity,” a new erotic thriller featuring the ubi
body:
SPOILER ALERT: This article contains spoilers for “Verity,” now playing in theaters.

	To say that “Verity,” a new erotic thriller featuring the ubiquitous Anne Hathaway and Dakota Johnson — who gets to call the former “a selfish, Machiavellian cunt” — has sharply divided critics would be an understatement. This thing has taken a bigger beating than a piece of beef hanging in Rocky Balboa’s meat locker (our own critic called it a “a flat-footed dud”). And the majority of the film’s detractors took issue with its ending. (It is still predicted to win the box office weekend, becoming Hathaway’s third No. 1 movie this year.)
	

	Directed by Michael Showalter (“Search Party”) and adapted from Colleen Hoover’s bestselling novel, the film tells the tale of Lowen Ashleigh (Johnson), a struggling young author who’s recruited by Jeremy (Josh Hartnett), the hot husband of novelist Verity Crawford (Hathaway), to ghostwrite the final book in her popular series from their secluded (and palatial) house in the woods. You see, Verity suffered a recent accident that’s not only left her wheelchair-bound, but also unable to talk or move a muscle. Once Lowen finds a manuscript stashed away by Verity, however, she realizes her idol may be far more sinister than she seems.


	While Showalter took a number of liberties with Hoover’s source material, including eliminating one of the dead children — a move Hoover, who consulted on the film, called “the best change we could have made” — he’s kept the book’s ending largely intact, though he almost didn’t.
	

	Verity’s manuscript reveals that she was resentful of her two children — and how they’d pulled Jeremy’s attention away from her — from the moment they’d entered the world. One day, she took their son and daughter out on the lake in a kayak and, knowing the children couldn’t swim, capsized it on purpose, killing their daughter (the son miraculously survived). Lowen grows to hate Verity and feel deep sympathy for Jeremy after consuming their memoir, eventually fucking and falling for him. Only Verity is alive! She’s been faking being paralyzed and mute the whole time! Once Lowen and Jeremy discover this, he chokes her to death at Lowen’s behest and they dump her body in the lake.



	The action jumps six months into the future. As Lowen (now pregnant) and Jeremy are packing up the Crawford home, she finds a letter tucked under the floorboards claiming that the manuscript was merely a writing exercise where Verity was envisioning the darkest version of herself, and that after finding the manuscript, Jeremy attempted to kill her. Consumed by guilt, Verity acted paralyzed as penance, and to remain close to Jeremy and their remaining child.

	“We tried a hundred million different ways to end this movie,” Showalter tells Variety. “Figuring out how to end the movie was the biggest challenge and the last thing that we did.”

	“Verity” ends with pregnant Lowen and Jeremy driving off together into their new life as she looks out the window and ponders what the truth was regarding Verity, ultimately determining that it will always remain a mystery. But that wasn’t the ending that Showalter and his team originally intended.

	“There’s two very significant other ways that the movie ended,” he explains. “In one version, Lowen, in that car scene, has that moment where she says, ‘I don’t know who to believe. One thing’s for sure: Verity was a master manipulator.’ And then she puts on a pair of sunglasses, leans back, and has this very cat-with-a-mouse-in-its-mouth look, puts her hand out the window, and as they’re driving away and a song is playing, she’s making [waves through the air] with her hand. So, the idea is that Lowen is the master villain. And then, you cut back to Verity sinking into the lake and her eyes open.” Yes, Verity was still alive!
	



	

					Dakota Johnson and Anne Hathaway in “Verity.”
									©Amazon/Courtesy Everett Collection
	



	It’s an ending that seems more in line with the film’s campiness on its face, but Showalter says he couldn’t seem to get it to land the way he’d wanted.

	“We tried a hundred different versions of that — of Verity still being alive, and of Lowen being the dark phoenix, because we liked it and it was really, really cool,” he says. “It was this amazing moment of, Holy crap! Has Lowen been the mastermind the whole time? It was the ending we always thought we were gonna do and it was what we had planned on. So, not showing her put the glasses on was such a massive revelation to realize.”

	Showalter and the studio held a series of focus group screenings with audiences — a mix of those who’d read the book and those who hadn’t — and they kept getting the same specific feedback regarding the “dark phoenix” ending.

	“A lot of times, when you’re screening a movie [for focus groups] and you’re getting feedback, the feedback is generic. It’s like, ‘I didn’t like the ending,’ but they may not be able to really tell you why. And what we figured out was, it’s because they want Lowen to be in a place of uncertainty when the movie’s over,” he shares.

	Showalter continues: “It took us a really long time to realize the audience isn’t ready to make the kind of decision at the end of the movie that we had been giving Lowen. Lowen had this moment where she put on the sunglasses and was like, I don’t give a shit, and the audience wasn’t ready to go there with her. The audience wanted her to be like, What the fuck have I done? We realized the audience is Lowen and the audience wasn’t ready to put those glasses on.”

	Hoover was “open to changes” between the book and the movie but stresses she’s satisfied with the ending they went with. “I couldn’t be happier,” she tells Variety. “I feel like you walk away from the movie with the same feelings you walk away from the book with and that was what I was hoping we would ultimately end up with. Those screenings really helped.”

schema.headline: ‘Verity’ Had a Much More Twisted Ending. Then Came the Focus Group Screenings

title: 17 Best New Movies Streaming in October: ’The Invite,’ ‘Disclosure Day,’ ‘Evil Dead Burn’ and More
description:
Oct 2, 2026 2:26pm PT	
	

	
		17 Best New Movies Streaming in October: ’The Invite,’ ‘Disclosure Day,’ ‘Evil Dead Burn’ and More
body:
Oct 2, 2026 2:26pm PT	
	

	
		17 Best New Movies Streaming in October: ’The Invite,’ ‘Disclosure Day,’ ‘Evil Dead Burn’ and More
	
	
			


			
			
	

									Courtesy Everett Collection / ©Universal/Courtesy Everett Collection / Â©Warner Bros/Courtesy Everett Collection
	

		
	
				

	October is Halloween movie season, so it’s the perfect time for two of the year’s high-profile horror releases to debut on streaming platforms. “Evil Dead Burn,” the extremely grotesque ninth installment in the long-running franchise, premieres on HBO Max this month and should prove to be a big home viewing hit. For the indie horror lovers, Jane Schoenbrun’s instant cult classic “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma” arrives to on Mubi to stream after a buzzy summer run that kicked off at the Cannes Film Festival in May.

	For non horror lovers, summer movie season tentpoles “Disclosure Day” and “Minions and Monsters” are both arriving on Peacock this October. Neither movie set the box office on fire, but streaming should prove a popular destination to watch the latest Steven Spielberg alien blockbuster and the latest entry in the uber-popular “Despicable Me” franchise. A24’s “The Invite” was a huge success in theaters, meanwhile, and should keep the Oscar buzz when it debuts on HBO Max this month.

	Check out a full rundown below of the biggest movies hitting streaming this month.


			
			
	The Invite (Oct. 23 on HBO Max)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				
	Olivia Wilde’s acclaimed comedy “The Invite” arrives on HBO Max after earning a sturdy $58 million worldwide at the summer box office. Wilde stars opposite Seth Rogen, Penelope Cruz and Edward Norton in this story of two couples whose uproarious dinner party exposes the cracks in their relationships. Variety named “The Invite” one of the best movies of 2026 so far, calling it a “bravura dinner-party dramedy that’s like ‘Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf?’ remade by the Woody Allen of ‘Husbands and Wives.’”
		
			
			
	Disclosure Day (Oct. 9 on Peacock)
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Universal/Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				
	Steven Spielberg’s “Disclosure Day” arrives on Peacock after a $241 million run in theaters worldwide over the summer. Heavily touted as the Oscar-winning legend’s return to alien-centric science fiction (he is the master who gave us “E.T.” and “Close Encounters of the Third Kind,” after all), the chase thriller casts Josh O’Connor and Emily Blunt as a cybersecurity analyst and meteorologist who set out on a mission to disclose the existence of alien life to the world. Colin Firth, Eve Hewson and Colman Domingo co-star.
		
			
			
	The Death of Robin Hood (Oct. 16 on HBO Max)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				
	“The Death of Robin Hood,” from “Pig” and “A Quiet Place: Day One” director Michael Sarnoski, casts Hugh Jackman as an aged and battle-weary version of the title character, who now lives in self-imposed exile and is tormented by his past. Robin Hood gets a shot at redemption after befriending an orphaned girl. Jodie Comer, Bill Skarsgård, Murray Bartlett and Noah Jupe also star in the A24 release.
		
			
			
	Evil Dead Burn (Oct. 2 on HBO Max)
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Warner Bros/Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				
	“Evil Dead Burn” arrives on HBO Max just in time for Halloween movie season. The third movie since the “Evil Dead” series reboot in 2013 (and sixth film in the franchise overall) is directed by Sébastien Vaniček and stars Souheila Yacoub (“Dune: Part Two”) as a woman looking for comfort from her in-laws after her husband’s death. Their gathering at a secluded house quickly turns into a hellish reunion as the family members turn into Deadites.
		
			
			
	Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma (Oct. 2 on Mubi)
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Mubi/Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				
	“We’re All Going to the World’s Fair” and “I Saw the TV Glow” director Jane Schoenbrun returned bigger and better than ever this year with the Mubi-backed meta slasher dark comedy “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma.” Hannah Einbinder plays a filmmaker tasked with rebooting a horror movie franchise who gets in over her head when she seeks out the franchise’s original star, played with seductive wit by Gillian Anderson. The movie rocked Cannes in May before earning $8 million worldwide over the summer, making it Schoenbrun’s highest-grossing movie yet.
		
			
			
	Minions & Monsters (Oct. 28 on Peacock)
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Universal/Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				
	“Minions & Monsters” is coming to Peacock after an underwhelming summer box office run with $523 million, putting it on the lower end of movies set in the “Despicable Me” franchise. However, family audiences are sure to turn out in force for the movie’s streaming debut. Pierre Coffin, the series co-creator and voice of the Minions, and Patrick Delage directed the film, which is set in 1920s Hollywood and follows the Minions as silent movie stars who struggle to adapt to talking pictures. Naturally, chaos ensues when the yellow creatures accidentally release monsters out into Los Angeles.
		
			
			
	Animals (Oct. 9 on Netflix)
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Netflix/Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				
	Ben Affleck directs, co-writes and stars in “Animals,” a Netflix original crime thriller that could continue the Oscar winner’s streaming luck after “The Rip” became one of Netflix’s biggest movies of the year. The synopsis reads: “When their son is kidnapped, a Los Angeles mayoral candidate and his wife find themselves drawn into a web of deception. As they scramble to raise the ransom payment, they’re forced to make choices – and reveal secrets – that could tear their world apart.” The cast also includes Kerry Washington, Gillian Anderson, Adriana Paz, Ray Fisher and Steven Yeun.
		
			
			
	Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger (Oct. 9 on Disney+ and Hulu)
			
								
				
	Noel and Liam Gallagher get reflective, philosophical and foul-mouthed in “Don’t Look Back in Anger,” the acclaimed documentary that chronicles the brothers’ highly-publicized reunion and comeback tour in 2025. Cameras were given access to rehearsals, backstage and onstage, while the documentary also includes the first joint interview with the brothers in over 25 years.
		
			
			
	Sacrifice (Oct. 16 on Netflix)
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Netflix/Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				
	Netflix’s “Sacrifice,” starring the high-profile pairing of Chris Evans and Anya Taylor-Joy, marks the English-language debut of “Athena” director Romain Gavras. Evans plays a movie star trying to launch a Hollywood comeback after a viral meltdown. Taylor-Joy stars as the leader of a group of environmentalist radicals, who crash a black tie gala attended by Evans’ actor. This hostage situation quickly goes haywire. Vincent Cassel and Salma Hayek Pinault also star.
		
			
			
	Love of Your Life (Oct. 14 on Prime Video)
			
										
					Image Credit: ©MGM/Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				
	Rachel Morrison’s romantic drama “Love of Your Life” earned strong reviews after its premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival last month. Margaret Qualley stars as Maya, whose chance encounter with Charlie (Gabriel Basso) “sets in motion a sweeping romance and a future beyond anything she had imagined. When that future is suddenly upended, Maya is sent hurtling toward an unexpected new life — one that will force her to reckon with who she is, what she wants, and how to love again,” reads the synopsis from Amazon MGM.
		
			
			
	Masterplan (Oct. 16 on Prime Video)
			
								
				
	Stanley Tucci gets a star vehicle in Prime Video’s original heist movie “Masterplan.” The actor plays “a legendary thief who sets his sights on the Mona Lisa, recruiting two young strangers to help him — Chiara, a sharp Italian cybercrime expert, and Jay, a swaggering French explosives specialist — before revealing they are long-lost siblings… and oh yes, by the way, he is their father,” the synopsis reads from Amazon MGM. The supporting cast includes “The White Lotus” Season 2 favorite Simona Tabasco and Victor Belmondo.
		
			
			
	V/H/S Mixtape (Oct. 9 on Shudder)
			
								
				
	“V/H/S Mixtape” is the ninth installment in the long-running horror anthology series and features segments from Ernest Dickerson (“Tales From the Crypt: Demon Knight”), RZA (“The Man With the Iron Fists”), David Moreau (“Mads”) and Renee Zhan (“O Black Hole!”). Musician and director Flying Lotus (“Ash”) contributes music video interludes to the film, and debut filmmaker Tobias Forge contributes a music video. Heavy metal icons GWAR also make a featured appearance.
		
			
			
	The Housemaid (Oct. 9 on HBO Max)
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Lions Gate/Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				
	Sydney Sweeney and Amanda Seyfried powered “The Housemaid” to a hugely impressive $400 million at the worldwide box office this past winter. The success launched a new film franchise, with “The Housemaid’s Secret” now on the way for a December 2027 release. Sweeney is returning alongside director Paul Feig. New cast members include Kirsten Dunst and Paul Anthony Kelly.
		
			
			
	Tenzing (Oct. 16 on Apple TV)
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Apple TV/Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				
	Jennifer Peedom directs “Tenzing,” the Apple Original Films thriller starring Genden Phuntsok, Tom Hiddleston, Willem Dafoe and Caitríona Balfe. The synopsis reads: “Based on true events, ‘Tenzing’ chronicles the little-known story of Tenzing Norgay (Genden Phuntsok), a gifted Himalayan climber who, alongside New Zealand mountaineer Edmund Hillary (Hiddleston), became the first to summit Mount Everest. Encouraged by his wife Dawa (Thinley Lhamo), Tenzing finds an ally in expedition secretary Jill Henderson (Balfe). Together, they persuade Colonel John Hunt (Dafoe) that Tenzing belongs on the British climbing team, rather than merely serving it.”
		
			
			
	Hokum (Oct. 10 on Hulu)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				
	“Hokum” stars Adam Scott as the alcoholic author Ohm Bauman, who becomes an unlikely detective trying to solve the mystery of a haunted hotel in a remote Irish town. As answers get closer, Ohm is forced to confront the darkness that has made him such a curmudgeon. From Variety’s review: “Irish filmmaker Damian McCarthy enlists Scott to play a bitter American writer who grapples with his own trauma while fending off supernatural occurrences in this unnerving spine-chiller.”
		
			
			
	Doing Life (Oct. 2 on Netflix)
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Netflix/Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				
	Tyler Perry’s latest Netflix original movie is “Doing Life,” the synopsis for which reads: “A single mother fighting to survive and a reformed ex-con with untapped talent find in each other an unlikely second chance.” The cast features Naomi Baker, Jay Reeves, Tamberla Perry, Karen Obilom, Jasmine Sargent, Lucky Johnson and Danielle Moné Truitt.
		
			
			
	Lorne (Oct. 5 on Netflix)
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Focus Features/Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				
	Directed by Oscar winner Morgan Neville, “Lorne” is a behind-the-scenes portrait of the comedy icon and “SNL” creator Lorne Michaels. The documentary traces Michaels’ journey from a young Canadian writer to the force behind “Saturday Night Live,” the late-night sketch show that has shaped American comedy and pop culture for more than five decades. The film draws on exclusive archival material, plus candid interviews with Michaels and the comedians he turned into superstars.
		
	
	


	
		More from Variety

title: ‘Celebrity Traitors’ Star Richard E. Grant Accidentally Reveals He’s a Traitor to Cast in Premiere, Calls It the ‘Biggest Mistake I’ve Made in My Life’
description: Richard E. Grant almost immediately blew his chances on this season of “Celebrity Traitors” in what he calls the “biggest mistake I’ve made in my li
body:
Richard E. Grant almost immediately blew his chances on this season of “Celebrity Traitors” in what he calls the “biggest mistake I’ve made in my life.”

	In the first episode of the U.K. reality competition reality series, Grant was chosen as one of the first two Traitors, along with “Love Island” host Maya Jama. But then shortly after being chosen as a Traitor, Grant revealed his role to a room full of other competitors.


	Speaking with host Claudia Winkleman before being tapped as a Traitor, Jama said she wanted to be an “unassuming, warm and misleading traitor.” Grant, however, said he was “utterly ruthless” and would feel no guilt. “If I was lucky enough to be a traitor, it would be a dream come true,” the actor said. “In this game, the only power you have is being a traitor.”
	

	When asked about his status, Grant blurted out that he was a Traitor to several contestants, who appeared to be shocked. “What’s the point in being in the game if you’re not?” Grant asked rhetorically. (You can watch this scene on X as tweeted by U.K. TV journalist and Variety contributor Scott Bryan.)

	Comedian Joe Lycett encouraged Grant to back down from the statement and reassure everyone he was a Faithful making a joke. “I think you’ve done something that’s never been done in the game,” he said. “It’s a bold strategy.”

	After realizing his error, Grant told the camera, “That may have been the biggest mistake I’ve made in my life. I was so thrilled to be chosen that in my excitement I said I was a Traitor. I need to defuse all of the heat coming in my direction.”
	

	Grant also said he was “absolutely convinced” he would be going home. But model and actress Jerry Hall did not believe him. “I’ve known him for over 30 years, and he says and does eccentric things,” she said. “I think he is acting out because he hasn’t been chosen.”

	In spite of the slip-up, Grant survived until the end of the episode. The two Traitors were told they had a chance to recruit and could kill another contestant at the same time.

	The duo selected comedian James Acaster and University Challenge presenter Amol Rajan, who met with Grant and Jama to plead their case. Both selected said they could deflect attention after Grant’s earlier mistake. The episode concluded on a cliffhanger before he made his decision.

	Also competing on this season of “Celebrity Traitors” are actor Bella Ramsey, singer James Blunt, actor Julie Hesmondhalgh, content creator King Kenny, Little Mix’s Leigh-Anne Pinnock, actor Michael Sheen, actor Myha’la, broadcaster and math professor Hannah Fry, actor and presenter Ross Kemp, musician and actor Sebastian Croft, actor Sharon Rooney and comedians Joanne McNally, Miranda Hart, Rob Beckett and Romesh Ranganathan.

	The celebs are competing to weed out the murderous Traitors among them for a cash prize of £100,000 for a charity of their choice in Ardross Castle in the Highlands. The first season of “The Celebrity Traitors” aired in October 2025, and later streamed in the U.S. on Peacock.

title: Skydance’s Track Record: 20 Years of Tom Cruise, Mark Wahlberg, Action and More Action
description:
Oct 2, 2026 1:38pm PT	
	

			


			
			
	

									Illustration Variety
	

		
	
				

	Next week, Paramount and Warner Bros. will of
body:
Oct 2, 2026 1:38pm PT	
	

			


			
			
	

									Illustration Variety
	

		
	
				

	Next week, Paramount and Warner Bros. will officially combine into one mega-studio with a familiar name: Skydance. The deal is expected to close on Tuesday.

	“By combining them, we aren’t rewriting history — we’re equipping these iconic studios with a more powerful engine. Together, we are Skydance: a creative-first home for bold, quality storytelling,” CEO David Elllison wrote on X Friday when announcing the new name.

	But Ellison’s Skydance Media has been active since 2006, and has a track record of producing primarily franchise titles, action films and streaming fare, though its television slate is somewhat more diverse.

	Of course franchises like “G.I. Joe” and “Star Trek” will remain a priority for the new studio, but does Skydance’s track record indicate anything about where the new combined studio’s priority will lie? 

	It seems unlikely that the Warner Bros. label will give up making awards contenders, or that Paramount will abandon rom-coms. But one thing seems to be a given: Ellison is big on crowd-pleasers, action films and familiar franchises, some that are decades-old.

	Skydance have earned more than $8.7 billion at the global box office, a healthy haul for a relatively small player. But how will the name translate from a production shingle making a handful of films and shows a year to a massive combined operation that Ellison promises will release at least 30 movies per year? If nothing else, Mark Wahlberg probably doesn’t need to worry about his career prospects for a while.

	Here are five takeaways from Skydance Media’s earlier films and TV series:


			
			
	Skydance Plays Favorites
			
										
					Image Credit: Getty				
					
				
	Skydance plays favorites, and its favorite favorite is unquestionably Tom Cruise. Expect more collaborations between the action icon and Ellison, even if “Mission: Impossible” was put to bed (for now). They already have a “Days of Thunder” sequel on the docket. Also, important to note, thousands of Hollywood stars have formally expressed disdain for a combined Paramount-Warner Bros., but Cruise told “The Pat McAfee Show” that he’s confident Skydance is “going to deliver” on its promises of revitalizing the movie business. Another Skydance favorite is Mark Wahlberg, who led the two “Family Plan” films for the studio. Ryan Reynolds is a frequent collaborator as well, starring in “Mayday,” “The Adam Project” and “6 Underground.” John Krasinski is a Skydance regular. He played the titular superspy across four seasons of “Jack Ryan,” and co-starred with Natalie Portman in “The Fountain of Youth.” The last name to look out for is Arnold Schwarzenegger. He did two “Terminator” sequels and starred in two seasons of “Fubar” for Skydance.
		
			
			
	Skydance Is Now an IP Machine
			
										
					Image Credit: Skydance				
					
				

	One of the most valuable assets Ellison acquired in the merger was the Warner Bros. library and their toy box of IP. DC Studios, “Harry Potter,” “Lord of the Rings,” “Game of Thrones,” Looney Tunes and “Scooby-Doo” are now all property of Skydance. Iconic films like “Blade Runner,” “Goodfellas,” “The Goonies,” “The Matrix,” “A Nightmare on Elm Street,” “Ocean’s 11,” “Vacation” and “Gremlins” are also now in Skydance’s hands, all ripe for exploitation. It’s not hard to imagine any of these properties getting rebooted or retooled into TV series to help kick-start the slate. 

	Skydance Media was already producing films for franchises like “Mission: Impossible,” “Top Gun,” “Star Trek” and “Transformers,” which will certainly play a role in filling out Ellison’s promise of 30 films a year.

		
			
			
	Big and Small Screens
			
										
					Image Credit: Aimee Spinks/Netflix				
					
				

	Skydance Media certainly produced some of the biggest hits at the box office in recent years, from “Top Gun: Maverick” to “Mission: Impossible — Fallout” and “Transformers: Rise of the Beasts.” 

	But Skydance has also focused extensively on made-for-streaming films and their sequels. “The Family Plan” brought favorite son Wahlberg into a more comedic action role, and was a hit on Apple TV+, spurring the upcoming “The Family Plan 2.” Gina Prince-Bythewood’s “The Old Guard” proved popular on Netflix, and also begot a sequel. 

	But that doesn’t necessarily mean the new Skydance will lean more heavily into streaming than before. The terms of the merger state that Skydance’s wide release films must have a 45-day theatrical distribution period, and the company can’t release those movies on any subscription streaming platform — including Paramount+ — sooner than 90 days after they premiere in theaters.

		
			
			
	Action, Action and More Action
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Paramount Pictures				
					
				

	Pick a Skydance movie poster at random, and chances are it features a bloodied movie star holding a gun. Aside from a few early outliers (2010’s “True Grit” and 2012’s “Guilt Trip”), it’s been all action all the time from the Ellison camp. It seems Skydance fell in love with the genre, and its eventual favorite star, Tom Cruise, after the release of 2011’s “Mission: Impossible – Ghost Protocol.” Just a year later, Skydance and Paramount teamed again to attach Cruise to “Jack Reacher.” In the years following, Skydance produced films like “World War Z,” “G.I. Joe: Retaliation,” “Star Trek Beyond,” “Baywatch,” “Annihilation” and “Gemini Man.” Recent Skydance titles include “Mayday,” “The Family Plan 2,” “Fountain of Youth,” “Mission: Impossible – The Final Reckoning,” “The Gorge” and “Heart of Stone.” 

	Ellison has repeatedly deemed himself a movie fan first and an executive second. He’s also made it no secret that Skydance’s creative direction is largely aligned with his own tastes. In the settlement with the state AG’s, Ellison promised to maintain both the Warner Bros. and Paramount lots as separate entities. But as we learned on Friday, Paramount film heads Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein will oversee both movie studios. Greenstein came from Sony, but Goldberg has been with Skydance for decades. The question now is: How will they balance the prestigious history of Warner Bros., the studio behind “2001: A Space Odyssey,” “The Shining,” “Goodfellas,” and the most recent best picture winner, “One Battle After Another,” with Ellison’s crowd-pleaser approach?

		
			
			
	Skydance Television: Diverse Selection
			
										
					Image Credit: Sophie Giraud/Prime				
					
				

	Skydance series like the massively popular “Reacher” and its spinoff “Neagley” are extensions of the company’s core Jack Reacher universe. But other series have gone in different directions: “Grace and Frankie,” which streamed for seven seasons on Netflix, garnered numerous Emmy nominations for the Jane Fonda-Lily Tomlin comedy. Apple TV+ series “Foundation” totaled three seasons of ambitious sci-fi, and action comedy “FUBAR” on Netflix starred Arnold Schwarzenegger in his first TV series leading role.

	However, Skydance Television never quite broke through with the kind of Emmy-sweeping fare produced by Skydance’s new subsidiary HBO, so it’s probably a hopeful sign that the premium cabler will continue to operate independently. 

		
	
	


	
		More from Variety

body:
Rapper Future's Brother
                          FBG Casino Reaches Plea Deal In Huge Fentanyl Case
                          Facing Prison Time
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 2, 2026
                            2:35 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Future's brother, FBG Casino, cut a plea deal in his fentanyl case ... after federal agents said they found 17 kilos worth of fentanyl in an Airbnb-turned-stash house.
      
    
            FBG -- real name Rico Deville Buice -- pleaded guilty Thursday to conspiracy to possess fentanyl with intent to distribute.
      
    
            While the judge in the case has yet to sentence him ... the plea deal notes the mandatory minimum for the offense is 10 years -- with the maximum sentence being life in prison and up to a $10 million fine.
      

            Because his request to continue his pre-trial release conditions before the January 7 sentencing date was denied, FBG was taken back into custody.
      
    
        Waiting for your permission to load the Instagram Media.
      
    
            According to the criminal complaint, the FBI and DEA executed a search warrant in November 2025 on an Airbnb property they claimed FBG had used as his stash house.
      
    
            During their search, authorities say they recovered 17 kilograms of suspected fentanyl bricks, roughly $300,000 to $388,000 in cash, a Glock handgun and some ammo, an extended magazine, a money counter, and destroyed cell phones.
      
    
            Per the plea deal, the rapper agreed to forfeit $388,930 in cash, the Glock, the ammo, and the magazine.

title: Megan Thee Stallion Kicks Off Spooky Season With Her Iconic Pumpkin Head
description:
Megan Thee Stallion
                          Hey Pumpkin Head, It's Hottieween Time
body:
Megan Thee Stallion
                          Hey Pumpkin Head, It's Hottieween Time
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 2, 2026
                            1:47 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
      
        
              
    
    
            What's Spooky Season without Megan Thee Stallion stickin' to her now-famous pumpkin-head tradition?!?
      
    
            Fans and followers associate the start of October with Meg's iconic look, and this year she featured celebrity hairstylist Kellon Deryck.
      
    
            The tradition goes back to 2021, with the sexy rapper posting herself wearing a giant jack-o'-lantern head ... a sure sign spooky season is upon us.
      

                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            She brought it back in 2022, 2023 and 2024, and in 2025 she paired the pumpkin-head theme with Halloween-inspired nail art.

            Big Black -- one of Howard Stern's famous Wack Packers -- is dead ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            The NYC Medical Examiner's Office tells TMZ ... Big Black died of arteriosclerotic cardiovascular disease, a condition in which fatty plaque builds up inside the artery walls, causing them to narrow and harden.
      
    
            The M.E.'s office declined to say where or when he died, but the condition is considered a natural cause of death.
      

            Big Black -- whose real name was Ronnie Benjamin -- appeared on the Howard Stern show back in the day with fellow Wack Packer Lawrence Coward -- who Howard called the "King of All Blacks."
      
    
            Although Big Black was not a regular on the show, Howard would keep him for extended interviews when he was in the studio because of his brutal honesty about his bleak existence, which fascinated the Shock Jock and his audience.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            In fact, almost everyone who listened to Big Black's Q&A's with Howard and his sidekick, Robin Quivers, fell in love with the Bronx-born man, who was also smart and well-spoken.
      
    
            Big Black attended the elite Bronx Science High School and was a member of Mensa, but he ended up on public assistance.  
      
    
            He was known for Howard's probing questions about his sex life ... and for his on-air dynamic with Robin.
      
    
            Big Black was 64.
      
    
            RIP
